newsitem.title: ROMANIA: France's Chirac to press US on Romanian NATO entry.
newsitem.headline: France's Chirac to press US on Romanian NATO entry.

text.p: French President Jacques Chirac vowed on Saturday to try to persuade the United States to accept the admission of Romania to an expanded NATO in addition to three favoured ex-communist states.
Chirac told a news conference at the close of a two-day visit to Bucharest that the United States was the main obstacle to extending membership to Romania and possibly Slovenia.

The first Western leader to visit Romania in six years, Chirac repeatedly promised to back the drive by President Emil Constantinescu and his centrist government to beat the odds and enter the first expansion wave to be announced in July.
Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic are viewed as near-certain entrants to be named at a NATO summit in Madrid.
"This enlargement presupposes that beyond the three countries due to enter NATO -- Poland, the Czech Republic and Hungary -- a fourth and, possibly, a fifth should also be admitted," Chirac said.
"France will do everything possible to persuade our partners in the Atlantic alliance to ensure Romania's admission to NATO from the Madrid summit in July."

He discounted a suggestion from a Romanian journalist that Germany was most reluctant to take in Bucharest. "You spoke about Germany. It is not there that the biggest difficulty lies. What we must do is to persuade the United States to accept this."
He repeated that expansion "in good conditions" was linked to prior conclusion of an accord between NATO and Russia.
Chirac suggested earlier that the former Yugoslav republic of Slovenia could also be considered for quick admission.

Chirac has been cheered by Bucharest residents grown unused to the pomp of state visits under Constantinescu's ex-communist predecessor Ion Iliescu who was shunned by Western leaders during his seven years in office.

His every utterance has been laden with references to France's role in shaping the new Romanian state at the turn of the century and cultural links with eastern Europe's only Latin nation. Romanian radio and television have saturated their programmes with French music and films.

Chirac told reporters that Romania's bid for fast admission was justified by the new government's commitment to reforms, a treaty with Hungary burying old quarrels and its strategic position "to strengthen the southern flank of the Alliance".
Constantinescu said Romanian admission posed no threat of a "new divide" in Europe as its former Soviet neighbours, Ukraine and Moldova, had expressed no objections to NATO expansion.
Romania, he said, would make "historic sacrifices" to clinch a post-Communist treaty with Ukraine, held up by differences dating from World War Two.

Even students who lived only a short period of their lives under Stalinist dictator Nicolae Ceausescu, executed in 1989, made admission to NATO and the European Union central issues during an hour-long question-and-answer session with Chirac.
Chirac told a woman of 19 that enlarging NATO was part of rebuilding a Europe too long divided by communism.
Even Russia, he said, accepted the principle of expansion, but insisted on the separate agreement with the Alliance to allay worries on how its interests might be affected.
"Russia is concerned about the means and applications of enlargement...and one can understand that," he said.
"(Russian President Boris) Yeltsin is open to enlargement on condition that a prior accord is signed with Russia."
U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright acknowledged after talks this week in Moscow that no breakthrough had been achieved with the Kremlin over expansion.
